title: Hardened Heart?
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
prayer: Jesus, there are wounds I cannot heal by myself and people I still struggle to forgive. You know the thoughts I am ashamed to admit and the anger I continue to carry. I give them to you. When they return, help me give them to you again. Melt what has hardened within me. Restore what resentment has taken from me. Rekindle my love, my faith, my hope and my joy. Teach me to forgive as I have been forgiven, and let no injury, no person, no memory and no hatred possess a part of the heart that belongs entirely to you. Amen.
body:
Today's readings speak plainly about forgiveness. Sirach tells us that wrath and anger are hateful things and asks how someone can nourish anger against another and still expect healing from the Lord. Psalm 103 reminds us that God is merciful and gracious, that he does not deal with us according to our sins, and that as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our sins from us. Then Jesus gives us the command that leaves little room for interpretation: “Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also should love one another.”

Nothing seems hidden in these readings.

What is hidden is our hearts.

I have been wounded and rejected, more than once. I remember the *whens* and the *whos*, and often I am still left wondering *why*. Some of those wounds hurt enough that I learned to isolate them. I sometimes envision that part of my heart as cold steel—a scar that does not move as the rest of the heart beats, almost as though one wall has become seized.

I come before God asking him to release it. Melt this place. Turn it back into living tissue.

But some wounds remain incredibly painful. Sometimes a memory returns and my first thoughts are not forgiveness. They are vengeance. I have caught myself wanting those who hurt me to suffer—not something quick, but something painful enough that they might understand the pain they caused me.

And then I stop.

Because I hear what I am thinking.

I go before God asking mercy for my own inequities while carrying thoughts like these about another human being. There is something deeply uncomfortable about recognizing that contradiction. Sirach almost seems to put it directly before us: how can we ask God for the mercy we refuse to extend to another?

So I pray. I ask forgiveness for the thoughts themselves, and I ask God to relieve me of them.

And yet sometimes they return.

That may be one of the hardest truths about forgiveness: **wanting to forgive does not necessarily mean the feeling of forgiveness immediately follows.** We can make the decision and still discover that part of the heart hasn't caught up.

While praying the Rosary today, I came across words I have read many times, but today they landed differently: Jesus, help raise us. Deliver us from sin and evil. Give us your light and your joy. Rekindle within us love, faith, hope and the gift of prayer.

*Rekindle.*

Something that once burned can burn again.

Then Romans says something extraordinary: “If we live, we live for the Lord, and if we die, we die for the Lord… whether we live or die, we are the Lord's.”

Perhaps there are other kinds of death besides the death of the body.

Hatred can create a kind of death within us. Resentment can kill the joy in one corner of the heart. An injury committed years ago can continue taking something from us today because every time we return to it, the wound opens and the person who hurt us occupies that space again.

The person may no longer even be present.

But the injury is.

And suddenly I wonder whether forgiveness is only about releasing the person who hurt us. Perhaps forgiveness also releases **us**.

I don't completely know how to do that. I wish I could say that I prayed once and every hateful thought disappeared. It hasn't happened that way.

There are prayers, spiritual practices and resources that can help us when we cannot seem to move beyond something ourselves. Msgr. Stephen Rossetti, for example, offers prayers and online deliverance sessions that I have found worth turning toward. I mention this because sometimes we need help. We need prayer. We need the Church. We need other people. And sometimes deep wounds may require other forms of healing as well.

I cannot always control the first thought that enters my mind when an old wound suddenly appears.

But perhaps I can decide what happens next.

I can feed the thought. I can rehearse the injury. I can imagine vengeance and allow hatred to harden that place again.

Or I can bring it immediately to Christ.

*Here it is again, Lord. I still cannot carry this correctly. Take it from me.*

Maybe forgiveness sometimes happens exactly like that—not as one magnificent moment when everything disappears, but as the same wound being handed back to God a hundred times until one day we realize it doesn't hurt quite the way it once did.

I do not want to be a prisoner of hatred toward anyone. I want to receive and emit light and love, honesty and compassion. I want the whole heart—not merely the uninjured portions of it—to belong to God.

So perhaps today I shouldn't ask myself whether I have completely forgiven everyone who has hurt me.

Perhaps the question is simpler:

**Am I willing to let God begin healing the part of me that still cannot forgive?**

Because Christ is Lord of the living and the dead. And if resentment has created something dead within my heart, then perhaps this is precisely where I should invite the risen Christ.

Into the hardened place.

Into the scar.

Into the memories.

Into the anger.

And ask him to make it live again.

Let us look directly at whatever keeps us imprisoned and meet it with something infinitely greater: the love that comes from the heart of God—a love whose enormity lies beyond the boundaries of human understanding.
